title: Distant Barcodes
statement: The integer array `barcodes` describes a row of barcodes. Put them in a new order in which no two neighbouring positions hold the same value, and return that order. The result must use exactly the values of `barcodes`, each as many times as it occurs there. If several orders work, return any of them; the input always allows at least one.
constraints: At least one valid order exists (no value occurs more than ceil(barcodes.length / 2) times)
notes:
## Intuition

The value that is most common is the dangerous one: if it is not spread out early, its copies end up next to each other at the end. So, greedily, always write the value with the **most copies left**, except that it may not repeat the value just written. A max-heap keyed by remaining count gives the most common value quickly. To avoid writing the same value twice in a row, the value just written sits out for one step (`waiting`) and goes back into the heap only after the next value is written. A brute force could backtrack over every order, but that is exponential.

## Approach

1. Count each value's copies in `count`.
2. Push every `[remaining, code]` pair into a max-heap ordered by `remaining`.
3. Repeatedly `pop` the pair with the most copies left and append its `code` to `result`.
4. Return the previous `waiting` pair to the heap; it may be used again from the next step on.
5. If the popped value still has copies, it becomes the new `waiting` with one copy fewer; otherwise `waiting` is `null`.
6. When the heap is empty, `result` holds every barcode.

## Example 1, step by step

`barcodes = [1,1,1,2,2,2]`; the heap holds `[3,1]` and `[3,2]`.

- Pop `[3,1]`: write 1; `waiting = [2,1]`.
- Pop `[3,2]`: write 2; push `[2,1]` back; `waiting = [2,2]`.
- Pop `[2,1]`: write 1; push `[2,2]`; `waiting = [1,1]`. The same pattern writes 2, 1, 2.
- `result = [1,2,1,2,1,2]`. LeetCode shows `[2,1,2,1,2,1]`; both are valid.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log k), where `k` is the number of distinct values: each of the `n` steps does a heap pop and push.
- Space: O(n + k) for the result, the counts and the heap.

## Pitfalls

- Popping the top value twice in a row is the classic bug; the value just written must stay out of the heap for one step.
- Choosing values in sorted order instead of by remaining count fails, for example on `[1,2,2,2,3]`.
- With an odd length, the most common value can fill `ceil(n / 2)` slots, so it must start first and end last; the greedy handles this automatically.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | copies of each barcode value |
| `heap` | max-heap of `[remaining, code]` pairs |
| `higher`, `swap`, `push`, `pop` | heap helpers: compare, exchange, insert, remove the top |
| `result` | the order being built |
| `waiting` | the value just written, held out of the heap for one step |
| `remaining`, `code` | the popped pair: copies left and the barcode value |
